newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.S. seeks Zaire talks, rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks Zaire talks, rebels advance.

text.p: U.S. peacemaker Bill Richardson arrived in Zaire on Monday as international outrage mounted over the plight of Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Fresh reports of refugee deaths filtered out of the north-east, where Rebel chief Laurent Kabila has given aid agencies 60 days from Sunday to repatriate the Rwandans.
But Kabila's rebels -- accused of driving the refugees into the jungle and aiming for their extermination -- moved closer to Kinshasa, closing in on Kikwit, 400 km (250 miles) to the east.

Richardson, arriving in Kinshasa for talks with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, declared that "There can be no military solution to the crisis, but rather a negotiated settlement leading to an inclusive transitional government and fair and free elections,"

"I am also here because of our grave concern for the plight of several thousand refugees and displaced Zaireans. There is a humanitarian crisis here and the international community must respond," he added in a prepared Kinshasa arrival statement.
Richardson said he would meet Mobutu on Tuesday morning. He will fly south, on Wednesday to see Kabila in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city and centre of its vast mineral riches.

Kabila who returned there on Monday after a weekend trip to the north-east to try to calm the outcry over the refugees' fate. He told Reuters in the eastern city of Goma that he hoped Mobutu would make a peaceful exit from Zaire's politics but if he did not the rebels could settled the issue by military force.
Thousands of Rwandan Hutus returned to Biaro camp south of Zaire's third city of Kisangani on Monday, telling of a horrific slaughter that prompted their exodus last week.
"There was shooting and people were being attacked with knives and machetes. It was total panic," said one man who emerged trembling from the forest as the aid convoy arrived.
Dozens of corpses of those too sick to flee fighting between Hutu refugees, local Zaireans and rebel soldiers lay festering in the camp, 45 km (25 miles) south of Kisangani.
In Geneva, relief officials said they feared some 50 Hutu children had been killed after they were seized at a hospital in rebel-held Lwiro near the Rwandan border at the weekend.
The rebels, who took up arms in October in a dispute over nationality for ethnic Tutsis in Zaire, control over half the sprawling Central African nation at the heart of Africa.
Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, took a strong line over the Hutu refugees, blamed by the rebels for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda.

"There have been some reports of massacres and human rights abuses. This must end," he said, adding: "International aid organisations and the United Nations must have immediate access to people in need. During my visit I will press for this."
Kabila agreed on Sunday to give aid agencies access to nearly 100,000 Hutu refugees who fled camps in rebel-held territory when they came under armed attack last week.
But both the United States and U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan, who last week described the fate of the refugees as "slow extermination", rejected Kabila's deadline as unrealistic.
Rebel leaders predict the capital will fall within days. Army commanders say they will defend the city to the death.

Kikwit residents said government forces had deserted the town leaving it open to the rebels. "Kikwit is on the point of falling. There is no panic and people are calm," said one resident in radio contact with Kinshasa.
Mobutu and Kabila have agreed to meet but finding a neutral venue has proved a problem.

Kabila insists Mobutu come either to Zambia or South Africa. Mobutu, who is convalescing after prostate cancer surgery in August, wants a venue closer to home. Zaire has accused Zambia of aiding the rebels. Gabon has also offered to host the talks.
Mobutu, 66, has ruled Zaire since seizing power in 1965.
